set.statement: In a meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials of medications for methamphetamine or amphetamine withdrawal searched to December 2020 (nine trials of six medications, about 240 participants, six trials at high risk of bias), only six trials of four medications could be pooled; the ibudilast and varenicline trials and one modafinil trial gave no usable data on the review's outcomes. No pooled medication other than amineptine differed from placebo on any pooled outcome: discontinuation with any medication RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.40–1.23); with mirtazapine RR 0.96 (0.48–1.92); withdrawal-symptom scores SMD 0.17 (−0.43 to 0.77); global state (overall severity ratings, three trials), no significant difference. Amineptine, tested in two small trials by the same three investigators, may have reduced discontinuation (RR 0.22, 0.07–0.72; very low certainty; the authors write that it 'may reduce' discontinuation) and improved global state (two trials, 72 participants; low certainty by the review's rating), although the review prints its global-state figures in two inconsistent versions; according to the review it was withdrawn from the market in 1999 after reports of liver toxicity and non-medical use, and the two case reports cited for this predate the stated year. Outside the pooled outcomes, single small trials reported less fatigue on amantadine, faster visual reaction time but no other cognitive benefit on varenicline, and better scores on 2 of 12 measures of a sustained-attention test on ibudilast, while two mirtazapine trials found no benefit for sleep, one reporting more night awakenings than placebo. Only one trial reported adverse events by arm. The two mirtazapine trials here treated the withdrawal period, over two weeks, and are not the longer trials of mirtazapine for methamphetamine dependence reported in a separate claim in this section.
set.plain: Nine small trials have tested six medicines for meth or amphetamine withdrawal, the low mood, tiredness, sleep changes and craving after stopping. Only six of them, testing four medicines, could be combined. Of those medicines, none clearly helped compared with a placebo, apart from one drug that is no longer sold. Single trials reported a few narrower effects, such as less tiredness on amantadine, and one found more waking at night on mirtazapine. The trials were so few, small and flawed that a benefit cannot be ruled out either, and the medicines' side effects were rarely reported. These short mirtazapine trials are separate from the longer trials of mirtazapine for meth use described elsewhere in this section.
